title: Zazen, Non-duality and Interconnectedness
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of cultivating mindfulness and awareness in everyday life through Zazen practice, which is not just about achieving enlightenment but also about transcending intellectual understanding and ritualistic behavior. Dogen's teachings on non-dual nature and interconnectedness highlight that all aspects of existence are intertwined, cutting through delusions to reveal a deeper reality. By embracing this perspective, one can transcend dualistic thinking and recognize the interconnectedness of all beings, leading to a more profound understanding of oneself and the world.

sentences.text: *An unsurpassed penetrating and perfect dharma is rarely met with even in a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the [unclear: "tatakara's"] words.*
My dear friends, my heart goes out to [unclear: "Sesshin"], to Zelda, her relatives, all the people who cared for her, and all the people who care for the people who care for her.
Because we are not alone.
Even though we see ourselves as individuals, we are so very connected.
There is no escaping from that connection.
And it really moves us when we know that someone was so hurt and under-resourced that they just couldn't make it.
So the heart goes out to everybody who knew Zelda well.
In my talk, I started out, "I'm so happy to see you here tonight," and I am, because we are still here.
And as long as people remember and people keep their heart open, nobody ever leaves us.
Now I'm going to go on with my dharma talk that was written in a happier frame of thought, because summer is calling.
If you should find yourself vacationing or traveling, please don't dismiss the joy you feel by being too serious.
Zen practice definitely does not ask us to ignore the beauty in life.
We appreciate and we love.
Also, we know that this moment, this day, this season will change and pass.
Tonight, continuing with our Dogen series, I thought that we could look at several essays from a different perspective.
Instead of looking at each essay and asking what it is trying to tell me, I grabbed a few and looked at them.
I was curious what the unifying facts were, what Dogen is telling us in so many of his fascicles.
I will bring up some common elements.
Mostly I looked at Fukanzazengi, the universal recommendation for Zazen, Zenki, undivided activity, and Zazenshin, the needle of Zazen or the point of Zazen or the lancet of Zazen.
Selectively, they are good samples to express the central role of Zazen in our practice, the non-dual nature of reality and the interconnectedness of all phenomena.
They also provide practical guidance for practitioners and give us a feeling for the universality and the transformative power of Zazen.
So these are the common elements I came up with.
Zengi is a little bit of an outlier, but it felt like I wanted to bring it into this conversation.
All three texts highlight the centrality of Zazen in Dogen's teachings.
Zazen is portrayed as the primary practice for realizing enlightenment and the essence of Zen Buddhism.
It's a primary practice, but it is not a program.
You sit so many hours of Zazen, you count your breath that well, or whatever you do, and you've got it.
But it's more elusive without the practice.
Another common theme in these fascicles is the non-dual nature of reality.
Dogen consistently emphasizes that practice and enlightenment, life and death, self and other are interconnected and inseparable.
The interconnectedness of all beings and actions: even if we don't know, even if we will never know, the world as it is impacts us continuously.
Interconnectedness is a key aspect of Dogen's understanding of the nature of existence.
Then Dogen, of course, offers practical guidance, especially in Fukanzazengi.
Dogen tells us exactly what to wear, where to go, how to sit, how to breathe.
It's amazing.
We still do it the same way 800 years later.
So by writing a fascicle such as Fukanzazengi, Dogen really demonstrated his commitment to making the practice accessible and available for everyone.
Dogen emphasizes that this practice is universal.
Your background doesn't matter.
Your age doesn't matter.
Your education doesn't matter.
Your IQ doesn't matter.
It is the practice of all Buddhas and the path to realizing one's true nature.

Even though Dogen doesn't speak explicitly about mindfulness, especially as we understand it in light of the mindfulness movement, it is implied that the principles of Zazen should extend into all activities, again promoting mindfulness and awareness of every action.
So we all know by now that Zazen is the core practice of Sotozen.
We practice Zazen not to achieve any particular state, but to practice mindful presence and awareness.
It is a practice of just sitting and observing without any attachment to thoughts, feelings, external distractions.
To sit and just let thoughts arise and disappear without chasing them or rejecting them is also called shikantaza.
Being the observer in your own mind, Dogen considered Zazen not just a means to enlightenment, but enlightenment itself.
That's where that word practice-dash-enlightenment comes in.
It's one word, forget the dash, but it's a German thing to link words together, not so much in English.
Zazen is the authentic gate to enter the way.
It is also a practice that transcends intellectual understanding and ritualistic behavior.
It is a direct expression of our inherent Buddha nature.
Zazen is not a meditation technique.
It is the living, breathing expression of ourselves, our practice and enlightenment.
This practice transcends time and space, embodying the timeless truth of our interconnectedness with all beings.
We can touch on our inherent Buddha nature through Zazen and bring the spirit of presence into every aspect of our lives.
As we sit in Zazen, let us remember Dogen's teachings and embrace each moment as a manifestation of the way.
In doing so, we honor ourselves and our sangha, and we also remember Dogen's teaching and embrace each moment as a manifestation of the way.
Zazen is our reenactment of the Buddha's awakening under the Bodhi tree.
I've mentioned this before, but one of Dogen's key teachings is the concept of practice realization.
Again, not two things, but one.
This idea posits that the act of Zazen is in itself the realization of enlightenment.
There is no separation between practice and enlightenment.
They are one and the same.
This perspective, of course, challenges this notion of striving to get something as a future goal.
Instead, Dogen encourages us to see each moment of Zazen as complete and perfect in itself, embodying what we seek.
Dogen wrote this famous essay called Uji, often translated as "being time" or "time being."
In it he explores the relationship between time and existence, which of course includes our existence.
He asserts that each moment of Zazen is a manifestation of the entire universe, encapsulating all time and space.
This means that in the practice of our sitting, we are not merely sitting in the present moment, but connected to all moments, past, present and future.
This timeless quality underscores its profundity and its capacity to transform our understanding of reality.
For Dogen, Zazen was definitely not limited to the meditation hall.
In his teachings, Dogen frequently discussed the importance of mindfulness in everyday activities, such as eating, working, brushing your teeth, interacting with others.

By bringing the spirit of Zazen into our daily activities, we cultivate a continuous practice of presence and awareness, breaking down the barriers that we ourselves erected between meditation and mundane activities.
I'm still trying to find out exactly what the mundane activities are, but it gets more and more confused.
Dogen also emphasized the importance of sangha, the community of practitioners, in the practice of Zazen.
He believed that practicing in isolation can lead to misunderstandings and difficulties.
The community of teachers and fellow practitioners helped create an environment where Zazen can flourish.
The communal aspect is very important.
It's crucial for maintaining motivation, receiving feedback and deepening one's understanding.
We all know that despite all these beautiful, wonderful things, Zazen can be very challenging.
Dogen acknowledged the difficulties practitioners face: physical discomfort, restless minds, doubt.
He encouraged perseverance and faith in practice, reminding us that these challenges are part of the path.
In fact, without trouble, without challenges, I really doubt many of us would be practicing.
And I know you all have been hanging out here long enough to know that Zazen is not about achieving a blank mind or hunting down specific experiences.
Dogen cautions against such expectations, emphasizing that Zazen is about wholehearted engagement with the present moment, regardless of what arises.
Dogen often highlighted the profound simplicity of Zazen.
In Genjokoan, he writes:
*To study the Buddha way is to study the self.
To study the self is to forget the self.
To forget the self is to be actualized by myriad things.*
This teaching encapsulates the essence of Zazen as a practice of self-discovery and self-transcendence.
Sitting Zazen, we come face to face with our true nature beyond the constructs of ego and identity.
I want to read you the opening lines of Dogen's Needle of Zazen.
One thing that's funny, not funny haha, but funny: we blame Dogen so much for his writing about not thinking and non-thinking.
I bet, like me, most of you really blame Dogen for that.
But as you're going to see right now, he copied this, like so many other things, from his Chinese ancestors.
So this is the opening of Zazenshin, the point of Zazen or the lancet or the needle of Zazen.
*Yao Shan, great master Hongdao, was sitting.
A monk asked him, "In steadfast sitting, what do you think?"
Yao Shan said, "Think not thinking."
"How do you think not thinking?" asked the monk.
Yao Shan replied, "Beyond thinking."
Realizing these words of Yao Shan, you should investigate and receive the authentic transmission of steadfast sitting.
This is the thorough study of steadfast sitting transmitted in the Buddha way.*
So, more about what he had to say about criticism of thinking, not thinking, non-thinking.
*However, careless students in recent times say the endeavor of Zazen is completed when your heart is quiescent, as Zazen is a place of calmness.
Such a view does not even reach that of students of the lesser vehicles and is inferior to the teachings of human and deva vehicles.
How can we call them students of Buddha Dharma?
In present day Song China, there are many practitioners who hold such views.
The decline of the ancestral path is truly lamentable.
There are also people who say practicing Zazen is essential for those who are beginners or those who have started studying recently, but it is not necessarily the activity of Buddha ancestors.
Activity in daily life is Zen and sitting is Zen.*
*In speaking and in silence, in motion and stillness, your body should be tranquil.
Do not be concerned only with the practice of Zazen.
Many of those who call themselves descendants of Lin Chi hold such views.
They say so because they have not received the transmission of the right livelihood of Buddha Dharma.
Who are beginners?
Are there any who are not beginners?
When do you leave the beginner's mind?
Know that in the definitive study of the Buddha Dharma, you engage in Zazen and endeavor in the way.
At the heart of the teaching is a practicing Buddha who does not seek to become a Buddha.
As a practicing Buddha does not become a Buddha, the fundamental point is realized.*
So this fascicle says that Zazen is not just a practice, but it's the very heart of the practice itself.
It's the expression of our Buddha nature and the embodiment of enlightenment.
You seek what is asking you to seek.
You already have it.
Zazen expresses all this without words.
It is through Zazen that one directly experiences and realizes the truth.
I have already brought up the non-duality of practice and enlightenment.
When one sits Zazen, we're not practicing to become enlightened in the future.
Instead, we are manifesting enlightenment in this very moment.
This is one of the cornerstones of Dogen's teaching.
And then, of course, there is the metaphor of the lancet or the needle.
It can cut through and expose.
Zazen cuts through our delusions and exposes the true nature of reality.
Buddha nature is inherent in all beings.
Look around you.
You're surrounded by it.
Buddha nature is inherent in all beings.
It slices through the layers of ignorance and conceptual thought that do obscure reality.
In the lancet of Zazen or the needle of Zazen, Dogen provides practical instructions just like in Fukanzazengi.
These are also tools to keep us in a mindful frame of mind.

As long as we keep attention to our body, that our thumb tips are just touching, that we're not trying to squeeze the life out of them, or that they don't drift apart when we're daydreaming, there is a realization that fosters in Zazen a sense of compassion and responsibility towards others.
As one sees our place in the web of existence, Dogen acknowledges the importance of student-teacher-sangha relationships.
Together, it is easier to practice, and we get a lot of support from each other.
So let's embrace Zazen as a transformative practice that transcends time and culture, guiding us towards a realization of our true nature and the cultivation of compassion for all beings.
Last but not least, I would like to talk about the fascicle Zenki, "undivided activity" as Tanahashi translates it.
It starts out:
*The great way of all Buddhas thoroughly practiced is emancipation and realization.
Emancipation means that in birth, you are emancipated from birth, and in death, you are emancipated from death.
Thus, there is a detachment from birth and death and penetration of birth and death.
Such is the complete practice of the great way.
There is letting go of birth and death and vitalizing birth and death.
Such is the thorough practice of the great way.
Realization is birth, birth is realization.
At the time of realization, there is nothing but birth, totally actualized.
Nothing but death, totally actualized.*
*Thus, such activity makes birth holy birth and death holy death.
Actualized just so at this moment.
This activity is neither large nor small, neither immeasurable nor measurable, neither remote nor near.
Birth right now is undivided activity.
Undivided activity is birth right now.*
Let's talk after the talk.
It will be time for Q&A.
So Zenki, undivided activity or total function or total dynamic function, are other translations of the title.
It refers to the idea that all aspects of existence are interrelated and that every action is a complete expression of the entire universe.
For Dogen each moment and every action, no matter how mundane, embodies the fullness of all existence.
Zenki addresses the inseparability of life and death, activity and stillness, and the continuous flow of being.
It demonstrates deep insight into the nature of reality, and Dogen challenges us to see beyond dualistic thinking.
In Zenki, Dogen asserts that life and death are not separate, but are interconnected expressions of the same reality.
He states, "Life is the total activity of the moment, and death is also the total activity of this moment."
Life and death are not opposing forces, but part of a continuous flow.
Each moment of life and each moment of death is complete and whole, embodying the entire universe.
Dogen also brought that up in Genjokoan, that each moment is complete and contains the whole of existence.
He wrote, "When you ride in a boat and watch the shore, you might assume that the shore is moving, but if you keep your eyes fixed on the boat, you know that the boat moves."
This illustrates how our perspective changes our understanding of reality.
By seeing each moment as undivided activity, we see that everything is interconnected and constantly in motion.
Again, no separation between self and other, subject and object, action and result.
Every action we take is a manifestation of the entire cosmos.
This understanding encourages us to engage in our activities wholeheartedly with awareness, recognizing that each action has far-reaching implications beyond ourselves.
Dogen in one fascicle writes, "The entire world is one bright pearl."
It suggests that phenomena are interdependent and reflect each other.
Please do not forget that each and every action, no matter how small, impacts the whole universe.
We just cannot believe that we are this important, but we are.
This should foster a sense of responsibility and compassion towards others, as we are all part of the same dynamic activity.
Zazen is not separate from daily life.
It is the very expression of Zenki in each moment.
Dogen invites us to see the world through the lens of undivided activity.
Every moment and every action is complete and a dynamic expression of the entire universe.
By embracing this perspective, we transcend dualistic thinking and recognize the interconnectedness of all beings.
I did want to end the evening with a poem, but I changed my mind.
I wanted to read another poem, but I doubt I'm going to find it on the fly.
This is from the book *The Wild Will Call You Back* by Gina Poro.
This is the one I originally picked.
It's called "The Wild Will Call You Back."
*The wild will call you back.
Through half-remembered dreams and sunsets painted in burnt sienna and vermilion flames, she will call you back home.
The coyotes will wake you from your sleep with their clarion call to keep your eyes wide open.
How long have you been sleeping?
How much have you forgotten?
The wild will call you back.
She will hang you upside down and shake the nonsense from your pockets of your mind.
She will strip your soul naked, leaving you raw and exposed under the searing glare of the gods.
Offer up the holiness of your confusion and questions.
Dress yourself in fireflies and [unclear: "the two new senses to awe"] while you learn the slow seduction of courting your muse.
Brush the stardust from your wings and wipe the ocean from your eyes.
Flex your claws, stick your roots deep down into the fertile earth and show your thanks.*
*Gather pollen on your legs and speak in venom and honey.
Peel back your colonized tongue and let it hiss and purr and growl and scream.
Do you remember how to stalk as predator and how to surrender as prey?
The wild will call you back.
The owls know your real name and will call you from the darkness of night to dance under the moon.
Crack your heart open with your ancestors' bones and dance in the ecstasies of your love and your grief with flailing limbs, bloody knees and mud-stained feet.
Braid [unclear: "mudward"] into your hair and dream yourself awake.*
*The wild will call you back.
She will teach you how to die again and again and how to die well.
There is no difference between your funeral pyre and your birth canal.
Do not bother to try and stop the pleading.
Love with the gentleness and ferocity of your whole soft, tender being.
Feed the spirits with your body, with your beauty and sweetness and ask them to show you the way home.*
*May our intentions equally extend to every being in place with the true merit of Buddha's way.
Beings are numberless.
I vow to save them.
Delusions are inexhaustible.
I vow to end them. [unclear: "Norma gates"] are boundless.
I vow to end them.
This place is unsurpassable.
I vow to become it.*

In Zenki, Dogen asserts that life and death are not separate, but are interconnected expressions of the same reality. He states, life is the total activity of the moment, and death is also the total activity of this moment. Life and death are not opposing forces, but part of a continuous flow.

Each moment of life and each moment of death is complete and whole, embodying the entire universe. Dogen also brought that up in Gensokyoan, that each moment is complete and contains the whole of existence. He wrote, when you ride in a boat and watch the shore, you might assume that the shore is moving, but if you keep your eyes fixed on the boat, you know that the boat moves. This illustrates how our perspective changes our understanding of reality. By seeing each moment as undivided activity, we see that everything is interconnected and constantly in motion. Again, no separation between self and other, subject and object, action and result. Every action we take is a manifestation of the entire cosmos.

This understanding encourages us to engage in our activities wholeheartedly with awareness, recognizing that each action has far-reaching implications beyond our self. Dogen in one fascicle writes, the entire world is one bright pearl. It suggests that phenomena are interdependent and reflect each other. Please do not forget that each and every action, no matter how small, impacts the whole universe. We just cannot believe that we are this important, but we are. This should foster a sense of responsibility and compassion towards others, as we are all part of the same dynamic activity.

Zazen is not separate from daily life. It is the very expression of Zenki in each moment. Dogen invites us to see the world through the lens of undivided activity. Every moment and every action is complete and a dynamic expression of the entire universe. By embracing this perspective, we transcend dualistic thinking and recognize the interconnectedness of all beings. I did want to end the evening with a poem, but I changed my mind. I wanted to read another poem, but I doubt I'm going to find it on the fly.

This is from the book The Wild Will Call You Back by Gina Poro. This is the one I originally picked. It's called The Wild Will Call You Back. The wild will call you back. Through half-remembered dreams and sunsets painted in burnt sienna and vermilion flames, she will call you back home. The coyotes will wake you from your sleep with their clarion call to keep your eyes wide open. How long have you been sleeping?

How much have you forgotten? The wild will call you back. She will hang you upside down and shake the nonsense from your pockets of your mind. She will strip your soul naked, leaving you raw and exposed under the searing glare of the gods. Offer up the holiness of your confusion and questions. Dress yourself in fireflies and the two new senses to awe while you learn the slow seduction of courting your muse. Brush the stardust from your wings and wipe the ocean from your eyes. Flex your claws, stick your roots deep down into the fertile earth and show your thanks.

Gather pollen on your legs and speak in venom and honey. Peel back your colonized tongue and let it hiss and purr and growl and scream. Do you remember how to stalk as predator and how to surrender as prey? The wild will call you back. The owls know your real name and will call you. From the darkness of night to dance under the moon. Crack your heart open with your ancestors' bones and dance in the ecstasies of your love and your grief with flailing limbs, bloody knees and mud-stained feet. Braid mudward into your hair and dream yourself awake.

The wild will call you back. She will teach you how to die again and again and how to die well. There is no difference between your funeral pyre and your birth canal. Do not bother to try and stop the pleading. Love with the gentleness and ferocity of your whole soft, tender being. Feed the spirits with your body, with your beauty and sweetness and ask them to show you the way home. May our intentions equally extend to every being in place with the true merit of Buddha's way. Beings are numberless. I vow to save them. Delusions are inexhaustible. I vow to end them.
Norma gates are boundless. I vow to end them. This place is unsurpassable. I vow to become it.
